ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Thickness Survey | Spokane, WA
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Spokane, WA for storage tanks, vessels, piping and structural steel. Mobilized techs. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Spokane, Washington
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in Spokane, Washington: wall-thickness surveys on storage tanks, pressure vessels and process piping, and shear-wave examination of structural and pressure-boundary welds. Technicians are mobilized to your plant, terminal or fabrication shop with calibrated flaw detectors and thickness gauges, and every reading is reported against the code or specification you name. Describe the equipment through the Spokane UT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Spokane

Spokane sits at the center of the Inland Northwest, and its industrial base is more varied than a first look suggests. The valley east of the city holds aluminum production and the machinery that casts and processes it, precision metal fabricators, specialty chemical and electronic-materials plants, and a growing mass timber operation. Recycling and used-fluids processors operate there too. Each of those sites runs steel and aluminum equipment whose walls thin in service, which is exactly the problem ultrasonic thickness testing is built to measure.

The typical assets are easy to list. Aboveground tanks hold fuel, process liquids, water and chemicals at bulk plants and industrial sites. Pressure vessels include air receivers, heat exchanger shells, deaerators and reactor vessels. Piping carries steam, condensate, compressed gas and corrosive process fluids. Structural steel includes crane runway girders, pipe racks, equipment frames, bridges over the Spokane River and the groove welds that join all of them. A thickness survey answers whether the wall is still thicker than the minimum the owner has calculated, and a weld examination answers whether a fabrication weld contains planar flaws that a visual check cannot see.

What ultrasonic testing finds, and what it cannot

A transducer sends short sound pulses into the metal and listens for the echo. In a thickness measurement the time between the front surface and the back wall, multiplied by the sound velocity for that material, gives the remaining wall. In a weld examination an angled beam travels through the weld volume and reflects from lack of fusion, cracks, slag lines and incomplete penetration. The method sees through the whole thickness, which is why it is the standard answer for internal corrosion that cannot be seen from outside.

It has limits that matter on Spokane equipment. Sound needs a coupled, reasonably smooth surface, so heavy scale, flaking paint and rough weld caps must be dressed first. Coarse-grained cast material and some austenitic stainless welds scatter sound and need special procedures. Aluminum has a different sound velocity from steel, so a gauge calibrated on steel will read wrong on an aluminum wall, and calibration on a block of the same alloy is not optional. Pitting is the hardest case: a gauge that reads at the bottom of one pit can miss the deepest pit a few millimeters away, so the survey pattern and the reported minimum must be understood together.

Storage tanks and the ASME and API picture in Spokane

Tank questions come up in Spokane searches more than almost any other UT topic, so they get their own section. Shell courses of an aboveground tank are surveyed in vertical lines at several elevations so the owner can see where corrosion concentrates, usually near the product-water interface, around nozzles and at the lowest course. Where the owner follows API 653, the authorized inspector sets the thickness locations and decides the remaining life and next interval. Atlantis does not act as that inspector. Our role is to take the readings, record the instrument and calibration, and give the owner clean thickness grids and a list of any area below the required minimum.

Roof plates, shell-to-bottom junction welds and nozzle necks can be measured from the outside. Bottom plates are harder: spot thickness readings from the top of the floor, where it is accessible, tell part of the story, but a full floor map is a different job from a spot survey, and we say so up front. Vessels follow a parallel path. ASME Section VIII Division 1 sets the design thickness, API 510 organizes in-service inspection, and Mandatory Appendix 12 of Section VIII governs ultrasonic examination of welds when the construction code calls for it. Piping owners using API 570 or ASME B31.3 rely on the same kind of condition monitoring locations, repeated at intervals so the corrosion rate can be calculated.

Codes and acceptance criteria that govern the work

Which document governs depends on the asset. ASME Section V, Article 4 covers ultrasonic examination of welds and Article 5 covers materials, while the thickness method itself is described in SE-797, which appears in Article 23. ASTM E797 is the matching consensus practice for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement, and ASTM E164 covers contact examination of weldments. Structural groove welds in buildings and equipment frames fall under AWS D1.1, which has its own ultrasonic acceptance classes and its own scanning levels. Steel bridge work falls under AWS D1.5.

The acceptance criteria are never ours to invent. The construction code, the owner specification or the engineer of record names them, and the report quotes them. If a pipe-rack weld is accepted under AWS D1.1 and the same technician reads a reflector that the Section VIII appendix would have rejected, the report must say which rule applied and why. That discipline is the reason procedures are written before the job starts rather than adapted at the pipe.

Washington's pressure equipment rules and Spokane

Washington regulates boilers and unfired pressure vessels at the state level through the Department of Labor and Industries, and the agency reports that it inspects and permits well over a hundred thousand units. A permit is required before a boiler or unfired pressure vessel is installed, reinstalled or moved. The City of Spokane ran its own boiler and pressure vessel inspection program until it moved to the state agency on July 1, 2026, and the city keeps its boiler operator licensing. Owners who dealt with city inspectors before that date should confirm with the state boiler program who now handles their certificates.

That change does not alter what ultrasonic testing delivers. The state inspector or the owner insurer's inspector still decides on compliance. What a UT survey adds is measured data: thickness at stated locations, weld examination results and the reference to the code that was applied. Repairs and alterations to pressure equipment follow the National Board Inspection Code, and the examination records from a weld repair feed directly into that documentation. OSHA's process safety management rule, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), also expects mechanical integrity inspections that follow recognized good practice, so chemical and fuel sites often schedule thickness work around that audit cycle.

How the technique is applied

For corroded steel the standard tool is a dual-element probe, which handles rough, pitted back walls better than a single crystal. The technician calibrates on a step block of the same material, checks the velocity, verifies at the start and end of the job and again if the probe or couplant changes. An A-scan display helps keep the reading honest: a thickness number alone can hide a doubled echo or a lamination, while the waveform shows it. Hot surfaces, such as steam lines or heated process vessels, call for high-temperature probes and couplant and a correction for the temperature effect on velocity.

Weld work is different. An angle-beam probe, typically 45, 60 or 70 degrees depending on thickness and joint, is calibrated on a reference block that holds side-drilled holes so a distance-amplitude curve or reference level can be set. The technician scans from both sides where access allows, sizes any reflector against the acceptance table, and sketches its location relative to the weld centerline. Where scanning is limited by geometry, for instance a nozzle weld with a short landing, the limitation goes in the report instead of being left to the reader to guess.

Who performs and reviews the examination

Atlantis technicians are qualified under the company written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The Level II technician who comes to your site calibrates the instrument, scans, and reads the screen. Procedure approval and report review sit with a Level III, who is not the person holding the probe. Our founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, which governs how the company runs its own management system, but the qualification of the individual technician rests on the written practice. An owner or code that names a different qualification scheme should say so in the inquiry. If your site needs a procedure written or a written practice reviewed, see our Level III consulting and written practice development pages.

What the Spokane UT report contains

Each report identifies the component by tag or drawing number, the procedure and its revision, the instrument, probe and calibration block, the couplant and the surface condition. For thickness work it includes a grid or table of readings by location, the nominal and minimum required thickness where the owner supplies them, and a clear list of readings below the minimum. For weld work it records the angle used, the reference level, the scan coverage, any indication with its position, length and amplitude, and the accept or reject decision against the named criteria. The technician, qualification level and date close the record. Reports are written so the owner's authorized inspector or engineer can use them directly without calling anyone to explain the notation.

Planning an ultrasonic job in Spokane

Spokane's seasons shape the work. Winter brings weeks of freezing weather, and couplant that works at room temperature stiffens or runs differently on a cold steel wall, so the technician carries a couplant suited to the temperature and checks calibration on a block kept near the part temperature. Summer sun can heat dark tank shells far above air temperature, so a probe that is comfortable at breakfast may need a high-temperature rating by afternoon. Outdoor jobs work best in the early part of the day in July, and winter jobs often move indoors or under a shelter.

Access is the other planning item. Tank shells need scaffolds or lifts, insulated pipe needs windows cut in the jacketing, and vessels need isolation and lock-out before anyone touches them. Plants in the valley run their own badging and safety orientation, and the crew should arrive with the training records the site asks for. Travel to Spokane is planned as part of the mobilization, since Atlantis has no office in the city, and a clear scope with drawings and a list of locations saves time on site more than any other single step.

UT compared with MT and PT for a Spokane job

Ultrasonic testing is the choice when the question is wall thickness or internal flaws. Magnetic particle inspection is faster and more sensitive for surface cracks in carbon steel, and our Spokane MT page covers that work. Liquid penetrant testing handles surface cracks in aluminum and stainless steel, which magnetic methods cannot, and the Spokane PT page explains it. Many jobs use two: a thickness survey on a tank shell and magnetic particle inspection of the attachment welds, or a UT weld examination on a new vessel and penetrant testing of an aluminum fitting. Our national ultrasonic testing page and the ultrasonic testing guide give the wider background.

Training your own ultrasonic technicians

Many Spokane plants prefer to train an in-house person to take routine thickness readings. Our UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training cover theory and practice, with the UT simulator for hands-on repetition. Certification itself is done by the employer under its written practice; see the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker for hours and prerequisites, and the Spokane NDT training page for how courses are delivered.

faq.q: Can you measure the wall thickness of a storage tank in Spokane?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians are mobilized to the tank site and take thickness readings on the shell, roof, nozzles and accessible floor areas, then report the grid against the owner's minimum. The authorized inspector decides remaining life and the next interval.

faq.q: Is UT acceptable in place of radiography for a weld in Washington?
faq.a: Only where the construction code and the owner allow it. Some codes include provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, while others require radiography. Agree the method with the owner, the engineer and the inspector before the job starts.

faq.q: Will Atlantis serve as the API 510, 570 or 653 inspector on my equipment?
faq.a: No. The owner's authorized inspector remains the inspector of record. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and reports thickness data, indications and the calibration record so the inspector can make the required decisions.

faq.q: Do you inspect aluminum with ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes, with a calibration block of the same alloy, because sound velocity in aluminum differs from steel. A gauge set up on steel will give wrong thickness on aluminum, so the procedure names the block and the velocity used.

faq.q: Who now inspects boilers and pressure vessels in the City of Spokane?
faq.a: The Washington Department of Labor and Industries took over Spokane's boiler and pressure vessel permits and inspections on July 1, 2026. The city keeps boiler operator licensing. Confirm certificates with the state boiler program.

faq.q: How cold can ultrasonic thickness testing be done outdoors in Spokane?
faq.a: It can continue in freezing weather with the right couplant, warmed equipment and calibration checked at a temperature close to the part. Very cold, wet or icy surfaces may call for a shelter or a different schedule.

faq.q: What do I need to send for a Spokane UT quote?
faq.a: Send the equipment list or drawings, the material and nominal thickness, the surface condition, insulation or coating, the governing code, the access arrangements and the dates you are aiming for. The more specific the list, the cleaner the scope.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Spokane?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in the city. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and the quote request is the first step. Travel and mobilization are planned into the scope rather than treated as an afterthought.

faq.q: Can my own staff be trained to take UT readings?
faq.a: Yes. Level 1 and Level 2 courses are available, with simulator practice, and your company qualifies and certifies the technician under its own written practice. Atlantis can help review that written practice if you need one.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Spokane, WA | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection (MT) in Spokane, WA for steel welds, cranes, lifting gear and structural steel. Technicians mobilized to site. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Spokane, Washington
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides magnetic particle inspection in Spokane, Washington, for steel weldments, crane and lifting components, structural steel and machinery parts. Technicians travel to your plant, yard or fabrication shop with yokes, particles and lighting, examine ferromagnetic surfaces to a written procedure, and report each indication against the acceptance criteria you specify. Send the part or weld list through the Spokane MT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection earns its keep in Spokane

Spokane has a long history of working steel. Fabrication shops build structural frames, tanks, platforms and machinery, and the aluminum and metals plants in the Spokane Valley depend on cranes, casting machinery and heavy handling equipment made largely of carbon steel. Freight rail corridors cross the region, and bridges carry highways and local roads over the Spokane River and its gorge. All of that steel carries welds, and welds crack where stress concentrates: at toes, at attachment points, at lifting lugs and at repairs made in the field.

The components that most often come up on an MT work list in a city like this are easy to name. Overhead crane hooks, lifting beams, shackles, sheave pins and trunnions are examined for fatigue cracks. Runway girders and bridge-crane end trucks have fillet welds that deserve a look after years of cycling. Pressure vessel nozzle welds, skirt attachments and lifting lugs are examined when the construction code calls for it. Rail car and heavy equipment repair welds, machinery frames, shafts and gear housings round out the list. None of these is exotic, and MT is the quickest way to prove them clean.

What magnetic particle inspection detects, and what it misses

MT works by magnetizing the part and dusting it with fine ferromagnetic particles. A crack or seam that interrupts the magnetic field creates a leakage field at the surface, and the particles gather there, making a visible line. The method finds cracks, laps, seams and lack of fusion that open to the surface or lie just below it, and it does so with high sensitivity and a result the technician can see directly.

The limits are as important as the strengths. The part must be ferromagnetic, which means carbon steel and most low-alloy steels, but not austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or titanium. For those materials, liquid penetrant testing is the surface method, and our Spokane PT page explains it. Deep internal flaws are beyond MT, and so is wall thinning from corrosion, which needs ultrasonic testing. A crack lies in one direction, and the field must cross it at a reasonable angle to make it visible, so each area is magnetized twice, in directions roughly perpendicular to each other. Paint, scale and grease reduce sensitivity, and thick coatings may need removal.

Codes and acceptance criteria for MT work in Spokane

ASME Section V, Article 7, sets the method requirements: the yoke or other magnetizing means, the particle type, the field strength check, the examination procedure content and the evaluation of indications. The acceptance rules come from the construction code. For pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1, Mandatory Appendix 6 gives the methods and acceptance standards, and ASME B31.3 process piping refers to its own acceptance table. Structural steel built to AWS D1.1 uses the code's visual and magnetic particle criteria, and bridges built to AWS D1.5 have their own provisions. ASTM E709 is the guide behind many procedures, and ASTM E1444 is the practice commonly invoked by purchase specifications.

Acceptance is never the technician's opinion. A linear indication of a stated length at a stated location is compared with the table that governs the weld, and the report records the table, the measurement and the result. When a specification is silent, the owner or engineer must supply the criterion before the job starts. A good scope names the code edition, the examination extent, whether surface preparation is by others and who dispositions a rejected indication.

Washington pressure equipment oversight and the MT record

Washington's Department of Labor and Industries administers the state boiler and unfired pressure vessel program, including permits and inspections, and it took over Spokane's city program on July 1, 2026. Repairs and alterations to pressure equipment follow the National Board Inspection Code, and weld repairs often require a documented surface examination of the finished weld. A clean MT report is part of the evidence that a repair was made properly, and it travels with the owner's records.

Lifting equipment has its own world. Crane components fall under owner maintenance programs and often under OSHA expectations for inspection of lifting devices, which is why Spokane plants schedule crane hook examination into annual shutdowns. The employer, not Atlantis, decides when and how often an MT examination is required. We perform it, report it and flag anything that needs the owner's engineer or the code inspector.

How the technique is applied

Most field MT uses an electromagnetic yoke. A two-pole yoke placed across a weld creates a field between its legs, and the technician sprays or dusts particles while the yoke is energized. An AC yoke must show a lifting power of at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing used, while a direct-current or permanent-magnet yoke must show at least 40 pounds, and the technician verifies this with a test weight rather than assuming it. Particles come in several forms: dry colored powder works well on rough weld surfaces and hot parts, wet visible particles in a spray can give more sensitivity, and fluorescent wet particles used with ultraviolet light give the highest sensitivity of all.

Fluorescent work needs a darkened area and a black light of specified intensity, so it is easiest in a shop or under a tent. Prods, where specified, pass current through the part itself and suit large castings and welds, but they require care to avoid arc burns on finished surfaces. After examination the technician cleans the part, and when residual magnetism would interfere with later welding, machining or bearing service, the part is demagnetized and the remaining field checked with a gauss meter. Cracks found are marked and photographed for the report.

Common problems found on Spokane steel

A few patterns repeat. Fatigue cracks start at the toes of fillet welds that attach lugs, brackets and stiffeners to girders, and they grow in a direction perpendicular to the main stress. Hooks crack at the throat and the shank threads. Pins and shafts crack at keyways, shoulders and fillet radii. Repair welds made without enough preheat show hydrogen cracks in the heat-affected zone, sometimes hours after the weld cooled. Heavy castings carry shrinkage lines and hot tears from the foundry. Knowing where to look is as much a part of the work as knowing how to magnetize, and the technician plans the yoke positions around those spots rather than sweeping at random.

Who performs and reviews the MT work

Examinations are done by technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up the equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications, while an ASNT Level III approves the written procedure and reviews the reports. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, leads that review. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If your contract requires a specific qualification scheme, state it in the request. For procedure writing or a review of your own written practice, see Level III consulting.

What the Spokane MT report contains

The report names the component or weld by tag or drawing number, the procedure and revision, and the surface condition at the time of examination. It records the magnetizing method and equipment, including the yoke's lifting power check or the current used, the particle type and color, the lighting measurement for fluorescent work, and the directions of magnetization. Each indication is described by location, orientation and length, then compared with the acceptance criteria, with the accept or reject decision stated plainly. Sketches or photographs help the engineer find the exact spot. The technician's name, qualification level and the date close the record. Where an area could not be examined, such as a weld too close to a wall for the yoke legs, the limitation is listed.

Planning a magnetic particle job in Spokane

Spokane's climate is dry and cold in winter and hot in summer, and neither extreme is neutral for MT. Steel at freezing temperature is fine for the method, but wet particle carriers thicken, aerosol cans lose pressure and gloved hands miss detail, so winter jobs often move indoors or use a heated enclosure. In July the problem is the reverse: surfaces in direct sun can become too hot for wet particles, which dry too fast, and dry powder or a shaded work area is the practical answer. Winds in open yards also blow dry powder away.

Fluorescent examination needs the ambient white light kept low, so jobs in daylight yards need a tent or a night shift scheduled with the site. Access, isolation and surface preparation are the usual planning items. Welds must be cleaned of slag and heavy paint, and scaffolds or lifts must reach crane girders and tank attachments safely. Plant safety orientation and badging take time at the larger sites, and because Atlantis has no office in Spokane, technicians are mobilized for the agreed scope and the travel is part of the plan.

MT compared with PT and UT for a Spokane job

Pick MT for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, where speed and sensitivity matter. Pick penetrant when the material is aluminum or stainless, and see the Spokane PT page. Pick ultrasonic testing when the question is wall loss or internal weld quality, and read the Spokane UT page. A typical fabrication job might use UT on the groove welds and MT on the fillets and attachments, with each result reported against the same code. The national magnetic particle testing page, the complete MT guide and the MT versus PT comparison carry the general detail, and the Washington overview is on the Washington inspection services page.

Training your own MT technicians

Shops that run MT every week often train their own staff. Our MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training teach the physics, yoke practice and indication interpretation, and the MT training overview explains the format. Your employer certifies the technician under its written practice, and the Spokane NDT training page describes how delivery works for a Spokane team.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be used on stainless steel or aluminum in Spokane?
faq.a: No. MT only works on ferromagnetic materials such as carbon and low-alloy steel. For austenitic stainless steel and aluminum, liquid penetrant testing is the usual surface method, and Atlantis can perform that too.

faq.q: What yoke strength is required for field MT?
faq.a: ASME Section V, Article 7 expects an AC yoke to lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds. The technician checks this with a test weight.

faq.q: Can you inspect crane hooks and lifting beams at my Spokane site?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your plant and examine hooks, beams, pins and welds for surface cracks, then report indications and acceptance decisions. The employer sets the inspection interval and decides on any repair.

faq.q: Do you use wet fluorescent particles or dry powder?
faq.a: Either, depending on the job. Dry powder suits rough or hot surfaces, visible wet particles give better sensitivity, and fluorescent wet particles under ultraviolet light give the highest sensitivity in a darkened area. The procedure states the choice.

faq.q: Does the part need to be demagnetized after inspection?
faq.a: Only when leftover magnetism would interfere with later welding, machining or bearing service, or when the specification asks for it. The technician demagnetizes and checks the residual field with a gauss meter.

faq.q: Which code decides whether a crack indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The construction code or owner specification, not the technician. ASME Section VIII Appendix 6, ASME B31.3, AWS D1.1 and AWS D1.5 each have their own criteria, and the report quotes the one that applies.

faq.q: How cold is too cold for MT in the Spokane winter?
faq.a: The method itself works on cold steel, but wet carriers thicken and aerosol cans weaken in the cold. Many jobs move indoors or use a heated enclosure, and the procedure states the temperature limits for the materials used.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Spokane?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in the city. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and travel is planned into the job. Use the quote request to describe what needs inspecting.

faq.q: Can my staff learn MT and be certified by my company?
faq.a: Yes. Level 1 and Level 2 courses are available, and your company certifies each person under its written practice following SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis can also review or help write that written practice if needed.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Spokane, WA | Liquid PT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Spokane, WA for aluminum, stainless steel and steel welds, fittings and machined parts. Technicians mobilized. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Spokane, Washington
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT provides liquid penetrant testing, also called dye penetrant inspection, in Spokane, Washington. It is the practical surface method for aluminum, stainless steel, nickel alloys and any non-porous material that magnetic particles cannot handle. Technicians travel to your plant, shop or yard, clean and test the surface under a written procedure, and report each indication against the criteria you name. Send the parts or welds through the Spokane PT inspection quote request and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing fits in Spokane

The Spokane area makes and handles a lot of aluminum. Aluminum production and semi-fabricated products, machinery for casting aluminum, precision fabricators and equipment repair shops all produce parts that magnetic particle inspection cannot test, because aluminum is not magnetic. The same is true of the stainless steel used in specialty chemical, electronic-materials and food or beverage process equipment, where piping, vessels and fittings are welded from austenitic grades. For all of these, penetrant testing is the surface method of choice.

Think of the parts that actually arrive on a work list. Welded aluminum frames, tanks and fixtures are checked for cracks and porosity open to the surface. Stainless process piping welds, tank nozzles and fittings are examined after fabrication or repair. Machined components such as valve bodies, shafts, housings and tooling are tested for cracks before they go back into service. Recycling and fluid-processing equipment adds welded repairs on mixed materials. Because PT does not depend on magnetic properties, one procedure can cover many alloys on the same work order. A single visit to a fabrication shop can therefore include an aluminum fixture, a stainless nozzle and a carbon steel repair, and the only difference between them is how the surface is prepared.

Surface preparation and why it decides the result

Most failed penetrant examinations fail before the penetrant goes on. Welds in aluminum are often cleaned with a stainless brush, which smears soft metal over fine cracks. Machined parts carry cutting oil in their pores. Stainless piping carries mill scale and weld discoloration, and painted equipment hides everything. The usual sequence is mechanical removal of scale or coating, solvent or detergent cleaning, and drying. Where mechanical cleaning has smeared the surface, a light etch restores the opening of the flaw. Parts must be completely dry because solvent or water sitting in a crack keeps penetrant out of it. A technician who skips this sequence produces a clean-looking part and a meaningless report.

Spokane shops that fabricate aluminum should keep brushes dedicated to one alloy, and stainless work should avoid carbon steel tooling that leaves embedded iron. These are small points, but they decide whether corrosion starts at a welded joint a year later.

How penetrant testing works, and what it can and cannot see

The principle is simple. A liquid with very low surface tension is applied to a clean surface and held there for a set dwell time, long enough to flow into any crack or pore that is open to the surface. The excess is removed, a developer is applied, and the developer draws the trapped liquid back out so it shows as a visible mark against the background. A color-contrast dye is read in ordinary white light, while a fluorescent dye is read under ultraviolet light in a darkened area and offers higher sensitivity.

The method is limited to discontinuities that are open to the surface. A crack covered by smeared metal, paint, scale or machining debris will not take up penetrant, which is why cleaning is the most important step, and why grinding, shot blasting and some wire brushing can hide the very defect the test is looking for. Porous materials such as some castings and sintered parts hold penetrant everywhere and give a useless background. Internal flaws and wall thinning are out of scope; use ultrasonic testing for those, as the Spokane UT page explains.

Codes, materials and acceptance for PT in Spokane

ASME Section V, Article 6, defines the penetrant examination: the allowed material families, the surface preparation, the dwell times, the removal method, the developer application and the evaluation. Acceptance comes from the construction code, so pressure vessels built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 apply Mandatory Appendix 8, and process piping built to ASME B31.3 applies its table of acceptance criteria. ASTM E165 is a widely cited practice for general industry, and many aluminum and stainless fabrication specifications reference it. Structural work to AWS D1.1 uses visual criteria with penetrant as a supplement when the specification requires it.

One material rule deserves emphasis. On nickel alloys and austenitic stainless steel and titanium, the specification often limits the sulfur, halogen and sodium content of penetrant materials, because residues can cause cracking at high temperature. The technician must use the lot-certified materials the procedure names and keep the lot numbers in the report. If a specification is silent, the owner or engineer should settle the question before the first part is cleaned.

Washington requirements and the records PT supports

Washington's Department of Labor and Industries oversees boilers and unfired pressure vessels at the state level, and it took over Spokane's city boiler and pressure vessel program on July 1, 2026. When a stainless or alloy vessel is repaired, the National Board Inspection Code expects documentation of the repair, and a penetrant examination of the finished weld is common. The inspector of record, whether state or insurance, decides acceptance of the repair. The PT report is the evidence the inspector reads.

Plants under OSHA's process safety management rule expect mechanical integrity work to be documented under 29 CFR 1910.119(j), and a surface-crack examination of a repaired stainless line is part of that documentation. Atlantis performs the examination and writes the report, and the owner or its authorized inspector makes the compliance decision.

How the penetrant technique is applied in the field

A typical job starts with cleaning. Solvent cleaning removes oil and grease, mechanical cleaning removes scale and paint, and the surface is allowed to dry fully because liquid trapped in a flaw blocks penetrant. Penetrant is then applied by spray or brush and left for the required dwell. Water-washable, post-emulsifiable and solvent-removable systems are all recognized, and field work most often uses the solvent-removable visible-dye system because it is portable and needs no water or power. Excess penetrant is wiped with a lint-free cloth, then lightly dampened with solvent, never flooded, because over-cleaning can pull penetrant out of a real crack.

After the surface dries, a thin even coat of developer is applied. The technician watches the surface during the developing time and again after it, because bleed-out grows with time and tells the size of a flaw. Indications are measured, photographed and recorded. Afterward, the part is cleaned of residue, which matters for parts that go into hydraulic systems, food service or high-temperature service.

Who performs and reviews the PT work

PT examinations are done by technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician performs the work and evaluates the indications, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the reports. What a Spokane PT report records

Each report names the component, the material and the weld or surface examined, together with the procedure and revision. It lists the penetrant system, the manufacturer and the lot numbers of penetrant, remover and developer, the cleaning method, the surface and ambient temperature, the dwell and developing times, and the lighting level for visible or fluorescent work. Indications are described by location, type and size, with a plain accept or reject statement against the stated code. A sketch or photograph accompanies anything rejectable. The report finishes with the technician's name and level and the date, and any area that could not be tested is listed.

Planning a penetrant job in Spokane

Temperature is the main planning point. The code expects penetrant testing to happen with the part and the materials between roughly the low 40s and the mid 120s in degrees Fahrenheit, and any job outside that band must follow a procedure that has been demonstrated at the actual temperature. Spokane winter mornings fall below the lower limit for months, and a steel or aluminum part left outdoors can be well under it even in a heated building if it was just brought in. Summer sun on a dark tank can push a surface far above the upper limit. The practical solution is to test in the shop or under a shelter, or to warm or shade the part until it sits in the window.

Humidity matters less in Spokane's dry climate, but dust does, because airborne grit settles on wet developer. Windy yards cause trouble for the same reason. Surface access must be planned: aluminum frames may need to be moved into a booth, and stainless piping may need insulation stripped and surfaces cleaned beforehand. Plant badging and safety training are normal at the larger sites. Since Atlantis has no office in Spokane, technicians are mobilized for the agreed scope and the plan includes travel.

faq.q: Can liquid penetrant testing find cracks in aluminum welds in Spokane?
faq.a: Yes, for cracks that are open to the surface. Aluminum is not magnetic, so PT is the standard surface method for it. Surface cleaning matters, because smeared metal can close a crack and hide it.

faq.q: What temperature range is acceptable for penetrant testing?
faq.a: Article 6 of ASME Section V defines a standard band that runs from the low 40s to the mid 120s Fahrenheit. A job outside it needs a procedure demonstrated at that temperature, typically with a comparator block.

faq.q: Is PT suitable for stainless steel process piping welds?
faq.a: Yes. Austenitic stainless is non-magnetic, so penetrant is the surface method of choice. Specifications often limit halogen and sulfur in the penetrant materials for stainless and nickel alloys, and the lot numbers are recorded.

faq.q: Does grinding or blasting affect penetrant results?
faq.a: Yes. Grinding, blasting and some wire brushing can smear metal across a crack and close its opening. The procedure often calls for etching or careful cleaning before testing so real indications are not hidden.

faq.q: Which penetrant system do you use in the field?
faq.a: Most field work uses the solvent-removable visible-dye system because it is portable and needs no power or water. Fluorescent and water-washable systems are used when the specification requires higher sensitivity or the parts suit it.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects an indication found by PT?
faq.a: The construction code or owner specification sets the criteria, and the technician evaluates against them. ASME Section VIII Appendix 8 and ASME B31.3 are common examples. The report states the criterion used.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Spokane?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in the city. Technicians travel to your plant or shop for the agreed scope, and travel is planned into the job. The quote request is the first step.

faq.q: How cold weather affects PT in Spokane?
faq.a: Below 40 degrees Fahrenheit penetrant thickens and the standard window no longer applies, so testing is done indoors, under a heated shelter, or with a procedure qualified for the lower temperature.

faq.q: Can my team be trained in penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. Level 1 and Level 2 courses are offered with simulator practice, and your company certifies each person under its written practice. We can also help review or write that written practice.
